title: Decimal Day: When Britain Changed Its Money Overnight

beats.say: Imagine going shopping, and the price is one pound, twelve shillings and sixpence. For centuries, that's how British money worked. Then, on one day in nineteen seventy one, it all changed.

cast.say: That's one pound, twelve and six, please.

beats.say: On the fifteenth of February, nineteen seventy one, Britain went decimal. It's known as Decimal Day. Overnight, a pound went from being two hundred and forty pennies, to one hundred.
Part one. The old money.

Here's how the old system worked. Twelve pennies made a shilling. Twenty shillings made a pound. So there were two hundred and forty pennies in a pound. It was called pounds, shillings and pence, or L S D.

And there were lots of other coins with wonderful names. The farthing, a quarter of a penny. The threepenny bit. The sixpence. The florin, worth two shillings. And the half crown, worth two shillings and sixpence.

cast.say: A tanner, a bob, and a half crown!

beats.say: People also had nicknames. A shilling was a bob. A sixpence was a tanner. And some posh shops priced things in guineas, worth twenty one shillings, one pound and one shilling.

vis.text: A bob, a tanner, and a guinea.

beats.say: You had to be good at maths. Adding up a shopping bill meant working in twelves and twenties. Children spent hours learning how to do sums in old money.

cast.say: Twelve and six, plus nine and four...

beats.say: Prices were written in a special way. Twelve shillings and sixpence was written twelve slash six. And one pound, twelve and six was written with a pound sign, then twelve, then six.
Part two. Why change?

By the nineteen sixties, most of the world used decimal money, counting in tens and hundreds. It was simpler, easier to calculate, and better for trade and the new computers businesses were starting to use.

A government committee recommended decimal money in nineteen sixty three. In nineteen sixty six, the government announced the change. A special organisation, the Decimal Currency Board, was set up to plan it.

The new coins arrived gradually. The five pence and ten pence coins came first, in nineteen sixty eight, because they were the same size and value as the old shilling and florin. People could use them straight away.

cast.say: This new 5p is just like a shilling!

beats.say: The ten shilling note was withdrawn in nineteen seventy, replaced by the fifty pence coin. The old penny and threepenny bit even carried on for a few months after Decimal Day.

vis.text: The ten-shilling note became a coin.

beats.say: In nineteen sixty nine came the seven sided fifty pence coin, replacing the ten shilling note. Some people hated it at first. It's still with us today.
Part three. The big day.
The date was chosen carefully. February was a quiet time for shops and banks. Banks closed for several days before Decimal Day, to convert all their accounts and clear cheques.

There was a huge publicity campaign. Leaflets to every home. Television programmes. Even a pop song about decimal money. Shops put up conversion charts, and people carried little converters in their pockets.

cast.say: How much is that in new money?

beats.say: Ireland changed its money on exactly the same day, because the Irish pound was linked to the British pound at the time.

vis.text: Ireland switched on the same day.

beats.say: Under the new system, one new penny was worth two point four old pennies. It sounds confusing, and for a while, it was.

vis.label: old pennies in one new penny

beats.say: On Monday the fifteenth of February, nineteen seventy one, Britain woke up to new money. Shops gave change in new coins. Price tags showed new pence. And it went surprisingly smoothly.
Part four. Old money, new prices.

Not everyone was happy. Many older people found it hard. And some people believed shops used the change to round prices up. Officials said overall the changes were roughly fair, but the suspicion stuck.
A famous phrase was born. How much is that in old money? People said it for years, converting new prices back into the old money they understood.

vis.text: 'How much is that in old money?'

beats.say: Some old coins stayed in use for years. The shilling and florin carried on as five and ten pence. The sixpence lasted until nineteen eighty, worth two and a half new pence.
Part five. The lessons.
Decimal Day is a brilliant example of a huge change done well. Years of planning. Gradual introduction. Clear communication. And a quiet day to make the switch.
And it reminds us that money is just a system people agree on. Britain's money had worked the same way for over a thousand years. And then, by agreement, in one day, it changed.

vis.text: A thousand-year system, changed in a day.

beats.say: So next time you see a fifty pence coin, remember. It's been around since nineteen sixty nine, and it once replaced ten whole shillings.
